title: Sport Pilot (Airplane)
summary: Free ground school for the FAA Sport Pilot knowledge test, oral exam and practical test, updated for the 2025 MOSAIC rule changes. Eleven lessons with self-check questions and a five week study plan.
who: This course is for anyone who wants to fly light aircraft for fun, with a simple route to the certificate: 20 hours of flight time for an airplane, a U.S. driver's license instead of an FAA medical certificate for most aircraft, and a 40 question knowledge test. A sport pilot flies in the daytime by default, carries one passenger, and stays at or below 10,000 feet MSL or 2,000 feet AGL, whichever is higher. Since the 2025 MOSAIC rule, a sport pilot may fly bigger and faster aircraft than before, and may add night, retractable gear and other privileges with training. The lessons teach the airplane category, with notes for gliders, gyroplanes and other categories where the rules differ. Rules are current as checked on the date shown below. Older study material may describe the pre-MOSAIC limits.

facts.label: Minimum age
facts.value: 17 to hold the certificate (16 for glider or balloon only)

facts.label: Airplane flight time
facts.value: 20 hours: at least 15 dual and 5 solo, with a 75 NM solo cross-country

facts.label: Medical proof
facts.value: A U.S. driver's license or a medical certificate (neither for glider or balloon)

facts.label: Passengers and money
facts.value: One passenger; no flying for pay; share costs, paying at least half

facts.label: Altitude and visibility
facts.value: 10,000 ft MSL or 2,000 ft AGL, whichever is higher; 3 SM visibility

facts.label: Aircraft limits
facts.value: Stall speed 59 knots or less for airplanes (45 for others); up to 4 seats in an airplane

facts.label: Practical test standard
facts.value: FAA-S-8081-29B Sport Pilot PTS, in use from September 14, 2026

notes: SPA is the code for Sport Pilot Airplane. Other sport pilot tests use the same size and score: SHF (helicopter with simplified flight controls), SPB (balloon), SPI (glider), SPL (airship), SPP (powered parachute), SPW (weight-shift-control) and SPY (gyroplane).
Each test has 40 questions, 2.0 hours and a passing score of 70. The FAA matrix lists 15 as the minimum age to take the test.

You need a logbook endorsement or written statement from an authorized instructor who trained you, or who reviewed your home-study course, before the test (14 CFR 61.307(a) and 61.309). A graduation certificate from an FAA-certificated pilot school also works.
Bring a valid ID with photo, date of birth, signature and physical address. If you do not have a Federal Tracking Number (FTN), create one in the IACRA system before you test.
The knowledge test report must be passed within the 24 calendar months before the month of the practical test (14 CFR 61.39(a)(1)). Take your report to the practical test.
If you fail, you must get more training from an authorized instructor and an endorsement before you retest (14 CFR 61.49). Bring the failed test report and the endorsement to the testing center.
The FAA publishes a test supplement (FAA-CT-8080-2H) with the figures and charts that the test uses. Study with it, and read the FAA's sample questions.
Practice questions can lag behind rule changes. If a question disagrees with the current 14 CFR 61.315 or 61.316, trust the regulation and ask your instructor.

practical_test.standard: Sport Pilot and Flight Instructors with a Sport Pilot Rating Practical Test Standards, FAA-S-8081-29B (June 2026, effective September 14, 2026), Section 1: Sport Pilot Airplane
notes: The sport pilot practical test has no separate ACS. It follows the FAA-S-8081-29B Practical Test Standards. Section 1 covers the airplane.

A pilot examiner gives the test. It has an oral part and a flight part. The oral part checks your knowledge of certificates and documents, airworthiness, weather, cross-country planning, airspace, systems, aeromedical factors, performance and weight and balance, and principles of flight. Area I of the standard lists these tasks.

The flight part covers ten areas: preflight preparation, preflight procedures, airport operations, takeoffs, landings and go-arounds, performance maneuvers, ground reference maneuvers, navigation, slow flight and stalls, emergency operations and postflight procedures. The examiner picks the tasks.

Typical limits: hold altitude within 100 feet and airspeed within 10 knots in ground reference maneuvers and steep turns; do slow flight and stalls no lower than 1,500 feet AGL; fly ground reference maneuvers no lower than 600 feet AGL; touch down within 400 feet beyond the planned spot for a normal landing and within 200 feet for a short-field landing; hold the best glide speed within 10 knots.

Before the test you need: your knowledge test report, the instructor's logbook endorsement for the practical test (you must have training within the 2 calendar months before the month of the test), a completed application, a medical certificate or a U.S. driver's license, and an aircraft that meets 14 CFR 61.316.

If any task in an area is unsatisfactory, the area is unsatisfactory, and the test is failed. You can retest after more training and an endorsement. The examiner records which areas and tasks you did not complete.
You can apply for a sport pilot practical test in a single-seat aircraft in some cases (14 CFR 61.45(f) and the standard describe the limits). Ask your examiner early.

requirements.text: Be at least 17 years old (16 for a glider or balloon only) and read, speak, write and understand English.
Get a student pilot certificate before you fly solo. A student pilot must be at least 16 (14 for a glider or balloon).
Hold a medical certificate or a valid U.S. driver's license that meets the conditions in 61.303, unless you fly only a glider or balloon.
Receive ground training from an authorized instructor, or finish a home-study course, on the knowledge areas in 61.309, and get an instructor's logbook endorsement.
Pass the SPA knowledge test: 40 questions, 2.0 hours, 70 to pass.
Receive and log ground and flight training on the areas of operation in 61.311.

Log at least 20 hours of flight time for airplane privileges: 15 hours of dual training and 5 hours of solo training, including 2 hours of cross-country training, 10 takeoffs and landings to a full stop, and a solo cross-country of at least 75 nautical miles with two landing points and one 25 nautical mile leg.
Log 2 hours of training with an instructor on the test areas in the 2 calendar months before the month of the practical test.
Up to 2.5 hours of qualified simulator or training device time can count toward the experience.
Get the instructor's logbook endorsement for the practical test, then pass the oral and flight test with an examiner.

plan.focus: Learn the certificate, its limits and the aircraft you may fly. Read the MOSAIC notes carefully, because older material is out of date. Take the self-check questions for both lessons.
Learn the medical rules, then the airspace classes, VFR minimums and the endorsement for controlled airspace. Draw the airspace classes from memory.
Study weather, then aerodynamics. Practice reading METARs and work the load factor and stall speed problems.
Study aircraft systems and weight and balance, then navigation and charts. Work three weight and balance problems and three navigation problems.

Study airport operations and radio, aeromedical factors and decision making, then emergencies and reporting. Practice radio calls aloud. Take the FAA sample questions and the practice test on this site, and review your missed topics. Then prepare for the oral exam with your instructor.

modules.title: The sport pilot certificate: steps, privileges and limits
modules.summary: How you earn the certificate, what it lets you do, what it forbids, and how you keep it current.
objectives: List the age, language, training and testing steps that lead to a sport pilot certificate.
Name the activities that 14 CFR 61.315 allows and the ones it forbids.
Explain why a sport pilot certificate has logbook endorsements instead of category and class ratings.
State the flight review and passenger currency rules that keep your privileges usable.

sections.heading: The path from first lesson to certificate
points: You must be at least 17 years old to hold a sport pilot certificate. The age is 16 if you only want glider or balloon privileges. You must also be able to read, speak, write and understand English. If a medical reason stops you from meeting the language rule, the FAA can add limits to your certificate instead of turning you away. To be a student pilot you must be 16 (14 for a glider or balloon).

The path has fixed steps. You train with an authorized instructor and learn the knowledge areas through instructor ground training or a home-study course. That instructor writes a logbook endorsement saying you are ready for the knowledge test. You pass the test, finish your flight training and experience, and get a second logbook endorsement from the instructor who taught you to fly. Then you take the practical test with an examiner.

Rule 61.309 lists what you must study. The list includes the regulations that touch sport pilots, NTSB accident reporting, the Aeronautical Information Manual and advisory circulars, chart reading for VFR navigation, weather and wind shear, collision avoidance and wake turbulence, density altitude, weight and balance, aerodynamics and aircraft systems, stalls and spins, aeronautical decision making, and preflight planning. This course follows that list.

Rule 61.311 lists what you must be trained to do. For an airplane the list is preflight preparation, preflight procedures, airport operations, takeoffs, landings and go-arounds, performance maneuvers, ground reference maneuvers, navigation, slow flight, stalls, emergency operations and post-flight procedures. The practical test checks the same areas.

sections.heading: Flight experience for airplane privileges
points: For single-engine land or sea airplane privileges you must log at least 20 hours of flight time. At least 15 of those hours are flight training from an authorized instructor in a single-engine airplane. At least 5 hours are solo flight training in the areas of operation in 61.311.

Inside those hours you need 2 hours of cross-country flight training and 10 takeoffs and landings to a full stop, each one flown in the traffic pattern at an airport. You also need one solo cross-country flight of at least 75 nautical miles in total. It must include a full-stop landing at two points, and one leg must cover a straight-line distance of at least 25 nautical miles.

You also need 2 hours of flight training with an instructor on the test areas in the 2 calendar months before the month of your practical test. Up to 2.5 hours of training in a qualified flight simulation training device or aviation training device can count toward the experience, if an instructor with the matching aircraft privilege gives the training.
These are minimums. Most students need more time. The instructor decides when you are ready and signs the endorsement.

sections.heading: What the certificate lets you do
points: With a sport pilot certificate you may act as pilot in command of an aircraft that meets the performance and design limits in 61.316. The next lesson covers those limits in detail. Your category and class privileges and your endorsements decide which of those aircraft you may fly.
You may share the operating expenses of a flight with a passenger. Only fuel, oil, airport expenses and aircraft rental fees count as operating expenses. You must pay at least half of them.

sections.heading: What the certificate forbids
points: Rule 61.315(c) is a list of things you may not do as pilot in command. Learn the list in groups. The first group is money. You may not carry a passenger or property for compensation or hire, fly for compensation or hire, fly in furtherance of a business, demonstrate an aircraft in flight to a buyer if you are an aircraft salesperson, or fly a passenger-carrying airlift sponsored by a charity.
The second group is people. You may not carry more than one passenger. This limit holds even when the airplane has four seats.

The third group is where and when you fly. You may not fly at night unless you have met the night rules in 61.329. You may not fly in Class A airspace. You may not fly in Class B, C or D airspace, at an airport in that airspace, or to, from, through or at an airport with an operating control tower, unless you have met 61.325. You may not fly outside the United States without permission from that country, and your certificate carries the limit "Holder does not meet ICAO requirements." You may not fly above 10,000 feet MSL or 2,000 feet AGL, whichever is higher. You may not fly when the flight or surface visibility is less than 3 statute miles. You may not fly without visual reference to the surface.

The fourth group is the aircraft. You may not fly contrary to the operating limitations on the aircraft's airworthiness certificate. You may not tow any object. You may not serve as a pilot flight crewmember on an aircraft that needs more than one pilot. You may not fly an aircraft that needs a type rating. You may not fly an aircraft with a VH above 87 knots CAS unless you met the endorsement rule in 61.327(b), and you need the training in 61.327(a) for an airplane with a VH of 87 knots CAS or less. You may not fly retractable gear or a manual controllable pitch propeller airplane unless you met 61.331.

The last group is personal. You may not fly contrary to any limit on your pilot certificate or medical certificate, any limit or endorsement from an instructor, or any restriction on your U.S. driver's license when you use that license as proof of medical fitness.

sections.heading: Endorsements instead of ratings
points: A sport pilot certificate does not list category and class ratings. After you pass the practical test, the FAA gives you a logbook endorsement for each category and class you may fly. Keep your logbook. It is your proof of privileges.

To add another category or class later, follow 61.321. For airplane single-engine land or sea, or a helicopter with simplified flight controls, you must pass a practical test. For other categories you get training and a logbook endorsement from your instructor. Then a different instructor gives you a proficiency check and signs a second endorsement.

If you hold a higher certificate, such as private pilot, you can still use sport pilot privileges. When you do, 61.303 sends you back to the sport pilot limits and endorsements. A pilot with a category and class rating for the aircraft being flown does not have to follow the sport pilot limits in that aircraft.

sections.heading: Keeping the certificate usable
points: A pilot certificate is issued without an expiration date. It stays valid until you surrender it or the FAA suspends or revokes it. You must carry it, with a photo ID, whenever you act as a required crewmember. A state driver's license is an accepted photo ID.

You need a flight review every 24 calendar months. The review is at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training with an authorized instructor, in an aircraft you are qualified to fly. The instructor endorses your logbook. A review in March 2025 keeps you legal through the end of March 2027.

To carry a passenger you need three takeoffs and three landings in the previous 90 days, with you at the controls. The landings must be in the same category and class. A tailwheel airplane needs full-stop landings in a tailwheel airplane. Night passenger flights need three full-stop night takeoffs and landings in the previous 90 days, counted from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise.

numbers.item: Minimum age for a sport pilot certificate

numbers.value: 75 NM total, two landing points, one 25 NM leg

numbers.item: Takeoffs and landings to a full stop

numbers.value: 2 hours within the 2 calendar months before the test month
10,000 ft MSL or 2,000 ft AGL, whichever is higher

traps: A test choice may say a sport pilot may never fly at night. That was true before the 2025 rule change. Today 61.329 allows night flight after 3 hours of night training, 10 night takeoffs and landings, one night cross-country, an endorsement, and a medical certificate or BasicMed.
The altitude limit is whichever is higher. Over terrain at 9,500 feet MSL, 2,000 feet AGL is 11,500 feet MSL, so that is your ceiling. Do not stop at 10,000.
A four-seat airplane still carries only one passenger when the pilot is a sport pilot.
Cost sharing does not mean the passenger can pay everything. You pay at least half of the fuel, oil, airport and rental costs.
Do not mix up the sport pilot solo cross-country (75 NM total) with the private pilot numbers. Use the 61.313 numbers.
Calendar months run to the end of the month. A flight review counts through the last day of the 24th month after it.

check.q: A sport pilot flies a four-seat airplane that meets the aircraft limits. How many passengers may the pilot carry?
choices: Two, if the pilot has a night endorsement
None unless an instructor is aboard
check.why: Rule 61.315(c)(4) forbids carrying more than one passenger, no matter how many seats the airplane has.

check.q: The ground under a sport pilot's route is 9,500 feet MSL. What is the highest altitude the pilot may fly there?
check.why: The limit is 10,000 feet MSL or 2,000 feet AGL, whichever is higher. At 9,500 feet MSL terrain, 2,000 feet AGL equals 11,500 feet MSL.

check.q: How do you show which category and class of aircraft you may fly with a sport pilot certificate?
choices: A logbook endorsement for the category and class
A separate FAA card for each aircraft
check.why: A sport pilot certificate carries no category and class ratings. The FAA gives you a logbook endorsement instead.

check.q: A passenger shares the cost of a flight with a sport pilot. What must the sport pilot pay?
choices: At least half of the operating expenses
check.why: A sport pilot may share fuel, oil, airport expenses and rental fees, and must pay at least half of the operating expenses.

check.q: A sport pilot passed a flight review in March 2025. Through which month may the pilot act as pilot in command without a new review?
check.why: The review must fall since the beginning of the 24th calendar month before the month of the flight. March 2025 is that month for March 2027, so the review counts through the end of March 2027.

modules.title: What you may fly: aircraft limits, MOSAIC changes and endorsements
modules.summary: The aircraft limits in 14 CFR 61.316, the extra endorsements that open more aircraft and privileges, and what changed under the MOSAIC rule.
objectives: State the performance and design limits an aircraft must meet for sport pilot use.
Explain the rule that an aircraft must meet those limits since its original certification.
List the training and endorsements for VH, retractable gear, a manual controllable pitch propeller, towered and controlled airspace, and night flight.
Describe how today's rules differ from the pre-MOSAIC limits so you can spot out-of-date study material.
Explain how a sport pilot adds another category or class.

sections.heading: Why the rules changed
points: In July 2025 the FAA published the MOSAIC final rule (Modernization of Special Airworthiness Certification). It separated two ideas that used to be tied together: how an aircraft is certificated and what a sport pilot may fly. Before MOSAIC, a sport pilot could fly only an aircraft that fit the "light-sport aircraft" definition in 14 CFR 1.1. Now the limits for sport pilots sit in part 61, in section 61.316.

The pilot rules in part 61 took effect on October 22, 2025. The aircraft certification side of MOSAIC, including the new light-sport category rules and consensus standards, applies to airworthiness certificates issued on or after July 24, 2026. The current eCFR text of 14 CFR 1.1 no longer contains the light-sport aircraft definition.

An aircraft can still carry a "light-sport category" airworthiness certificate, but that label no longer decides what a sport pilot may fly. Section 61.316 decides. A sport pilot can now fly some standard-category airplanes and other aircraft that meet the limits, as long as the operating limitations on the aircraft's airworthiness certificate allow it.
Older books, videos, apps and practice questions may still teach the pre-MOSAIC limits. If a source disagrees with 61.315 or 61.316, trust the current regulation and ask your instructor.

sections.heading: The aircraft limits in 61.316
points: Stall speed: the aircraft must have a stall speed, or minimum steady flight speed, without lift-enhancing devices (VS1) of no more than 45 knots CAS. Airplanes have a looser limit of 59 knots CAS at maximum certificated takeoff weight and the most critical center of gravity. CAS means calibrated airspeed.
Seats: no more than two persons, except airplanes, which may have up to four seats. Remember that the number of seats is not the number of people you may carry. You still carry one passenger.

Cabin and power: if the aircraft has a cabin, it must not be pressurized. A powered aircraft, other than a balloon or airship, must keep directional control if it loses partial power. It must also let the pilot set up a controlled descent after a partial or total powerplant failure.

Gear and propeller: a powered aircraft other than a glider must have fixed landing gear, and a fixed, ground-adjustable or automated controllable pitch propeller. A glider may have fixed or retractable gear. A gyroplane must have a fixed-pitch, semi-rigid, teetering, two-blade rotor system. A helicopter must be certificated with the simplified flight controls designation.
Sport pilots may also fly an aircraft with retractable landing gear, or an airplane with a manual controllable pitch propeller, after the training and endorsement in 61.331.
There is no longer a weight limit, no cap on maximum speed, and no single-reciprocating-engine rule. A sport pilot still may not fly an aircraft that needs a type rating under 61.31(a).

sections.heading: The "since original certification" rule
points: Section 61.316(a) says the aircraft must meet the limits "since its original certification." You cannot change an aircraft to make it fit.
Taking seats out of an airplane that was originally certificated with more than four seats does not make it eligible. The FAA's advisory circular says the original design and performance still count.
The same idea covers stall speed. Vortex generators, short takeoff and landing kits and other lift devices may be installed, but the aircraft's original VS1 must still meet the limit.

There is one exception. Landing gear and propeller changes are allowed. A sport pilot may fly an aircraft with retractable gear, or an airplane with a manual controllable pitch propeller, if the pilot has the 61.331 training and endorsement.

sections.heading: Extra training and endorsements
points: VH endorsement (61.327): VH is the top speed in level flight at maximum continuous power. For an airplane with a VH of 87 knots CAS or less, you need ground and flight training in such an airplane and a logbook endorsement. For any aircraft with a VH above 87 knots CAS you need the same kind of training and endorsement in an aircraft above 87 knots. A sport pilot who logged pilot-in-command time in an airplane with a VH of 87 knots CAS or less before April 2, 2010 does not need the first endorsement.

Retractable gear and manual controllable pitch propeller (61.331): get the complex-airplane training and endorsement in 61.31(e), or get ground and flight training in an aircraft with that equipment and an instructor's endorsement. A pilot who logged pilot-in-command time before October 22, 2025 in a water aircraft with retractable gear does not need the gear endorsement.

Class B, C and D airspace and towered airports (61.325): ground and flight training on radios, communications, navigation systems and radar services, three takeoffs and landings to a full stop at an airport with an operating control tower, and the part 91 rules for B, C and D airspace and ATC clearances. The instructor signs a logbook endorsement.

Night (61.329): 3 hours of night training in the category and class, including one cross-country flight with a landing at an airport at least 25 nautical miles from the departure airport (not required for powered parachutes) and at least 10 night takeoffs and 10 night landings to a full stop. You need an instructor's endorsement and either a medical certificate or the BasicMed conditions.

sections.heading: Old limits you will still see
points: The pre-MOSAIC definition of a light-sport aircraft set these limits: maximum takeoff weight of 1,320 pounds (1,430 pounds for an aircraft intended for water operations), maximum level-flight speed (VH) of 120 knots CAS, maximum VS1 of 45 knots CAS for every aircraft, two seats including the pilot, one reciprocating engine, fixed gear except for water aircraft and gliders, and a fixed or ground-adjustable propeller.

Today weight, the 120-knot speed cap, the engine rule and the two-seat rule for airplanes are gone. Airplanes may have a VS1 of up to 59 knots and four seats. Night flight, retractable gear and manual controllable pitch propellers are now possible with training.
The FAA's Airplane Flying Handbook chapter on light-sport airplanes still describes the older list. Use it for flying technique, not for current eligibility.

sections.heading: Adding another category or class
points: Under 61.321, a sport pilot (or a higher-grade pilot) who wants another category or class follows one of two paths. For airplane single-engine land or sea, or a helicopter with simplified flight controls, the pilot passes a practical test.

For other categories, such as glider, gyroplane, weight-shift-control or powered parachute, the pilot gets training and an instructor endorsement, passes a proficiency check from a different instructor, completes an application, and receives a second endorsement from the instructor who gave the check.

numbers.value: 3 hours, 10 takeoffs and 10 landings, one cross-country of at least 25 NM
3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop at a towered airport

numbers.item: Old LSA weight limit (no longer applies)
Old LSA speed limit (no longer applies)

traps: Do not use the pre-MOSAIC list as today's rule. The 1,320-pound weight limit, the 120-knot VH cap and the two-seat limit for airplanes are gone.
Do not mix up the 87-knot VH line with the stall speed limit. The 87 knots decides which endorsement you need. The 59 or 45 knots decides if the aircraft is eligible.
Seat count is about the aircraft. Passenger count is about the pilot. A four-seat airplane may qualify, but you still carry one passenger.
Removing seats or adding a stall-lowering device does not change the original certification. It does not make an aircraft eligible.
A "light-sport category" label on the airworthiness certificate is not the test. Check 61.316.
Night flight needs more than training. You also need a medical certificate or BasicMed. A driver's license alone is not enough.

check.why: Airplanes may have a VS1 of up to 59 knots CAS at maximum certificated takeoff weight. Other aircraft are limited to 45 knots CAS.

Check 61.316: it has no weight limit and no VH cap
Ask the examiner to ignore it
Use the weight limit only for airplanes
check.why: MOSAIC removed the weight limit and the 120-knot VH cap from the sport pilot aircraft limits. Section 61.316 is the current source.

modules.title: Medical rules: driver's license or medical certificate
modules.summary: When a sport pilot needs a medical certificate, when a U.S. driver's license is enough, when neither is needed, and what changes at night.
objectives: Tell which medical proof each kind of sport pilot flight needs.
List the conditions for using a U.S. driver's license instead of a medical certificate.
Explain the medical rule for night privileges, including BasicMed.
State your duty to stay out of the cockpit when you are not fit to fly.

sections.heading: Three situations
points: Powered aircraft, gyroplanes and other aircraft that meet 61.316, except gliders and balloons: you must hold either a medical certificate issued under part 67 or a U.S. driver's license. This applies to a student pilot seeking sport pilot privileges, to a sport pilot, and to an instructor or examiner who flies as pilot in command or as a required crewmember.
Gliders and balloons: a sport pilot, and a student pilot seeking those privileges, needs neither a medical certificate nor a driver's license.
Night flight: a driver's license alone is not enough. You need a medical certificate or you must meet the BasicMed conditions. The section on night privileges below explains this.

sections.heading: Conditions for using your driver's license
points: The license must be a U.S. driver's license, and you must follow every restriction on it. You must also follow any court or administrative order that applies to driving a motor vehicle.

If you ever applied for a medical certificate, your most recent application must have found you eligible for at least a third-class certificate. If you have been denied, you cannot fall back on your license.

If you have ever held a medical certificate, the most recent one must not have been suspended or revoked. Your most recent special issuance authorization must not have been withdrawn. An expired medical certificate does not by itself block you.
You must not know of, or have reason to know of, any medical condition that would keep you from flying safely. This last condition is on you. The license does not replace your own judgment.

sections.heading: Medical rules for night flight
points: Night privileges under 61.329 require a medical certificate issued under part 67, or the BasicMed conditions in 61.113(i), together with the training and endorsement described in the aircraft lesson.

BasicMed has its own steps. You must have held a regular medical certificate at some time after July 14, 2006. You must complete the medical education course in the 24 calendar months before you fly, and you must have a comprehensive exam by a state-licensed physician in the 48 calendar months before you fly. If a doctor has diagnosed a condition that could affect flying, you must be under that doctor's care while you fly.
Your most recent medical certificate under that route may be expired, and it may include a special issuance. It cannot have been suspended or revoked.

sections.heading: You are the final check
points: Medical rules are a minimum. A driver's license does not know that you have a new medicine, a fever or an unexplained dizzy spell. Ground yourself when you are not fit.

Rule 91.17 forbids acting as a crewmember within 8 hours after drinking any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence of alcohol, with a blood or breath alcohol concentration of 0.04 or more, or while using any drug that affects your faculties in a way that is unsafe. Eight hours is a minimum. Many pilots wait longer.
Carry your pilot certificate, a photo ID and your medical proof. A state driver's license can serve as both your photo ID and your medical proof.

numbers.item: Alcohol: hours before acting as a crewmember
Earlier medical certificate required for BasicMed

traps: A test choice may say every sport pilot needs a medical certificate. Most can use a U.S. driver's license, and glider and balloon pilots need neither.
A foreign driver's license does not count. The rule says a U.S. driver's license.
If your last medical application found you ineligible, the driver's license route is closed to you.
Eight hours bottle to throttle is a legal minimum, not a safe rule of thumb.
Night privileges need a medical certificate or BasicMed. A license alone does not work at night.

modules.title: Airspace, VFR weather minimums and the controlled airspace endorsement
modules.summary: The airspace classes, the VFR minimums, the sport pilot limits on altitude and visibility, and the endorsement for towered and controlled airspace.
objectives: Describe the shape and the entry rules of Class B, C, D, E and G airspace.
Apply the basic VFR weather minimums and the extra 3 mile visibility rule for sport pilots.
Explain what the 61.325 endorsement covers and where you need it.
Recognize special use airspace, temporary flight restrictions and the transponder and ADS-B rules.
Apply the right-of-way, speed and minimum altitude rules.

sections.heading: The classes at a glance
points: Class A starts at 18,000 feet MSL. A sport pilot cannot fly there, and the 10,000 foot altitude limit keeps you far below it anyway.

Class B surrounds the busiest airports. It usually runs from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL and looks like an upside-down wedding cake. You need an ATC clearance to enter, and VFR flight in Class B requires you to stay clear of clouds. Two-way radio, a transponder with altitude reporting and ADS-B Out are required unless ATC authorizes otherwise.

Class C usually has a 5 nautical mile core that runs from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport, and a 10 nautical mile shelf that runs from no lower than 1,200 feet up to 4,000 feet above the airport. You must establish two-way radio contact with ATC before you enter and keep it while you are inside.

Class D runs from the surface to about 2,500 feet above the airport and surrounds an airport with an operating control tower. You must establish two-way radio contact before you enter. If the tower closes at night, the airspace may turn into Class E or Class G. The Chart Supplement lists the hours.

Class E is controlled airspace that is not A, B, C or D. It often starts at 700 feet AGL (shown on the sectional chart with a magenta fade) or 1,200 feet AGL (blue fade). Some Class E starts at the surface around an airport. You need no clearance and no radio call to enter Class E.
Class G is uncontrolled airspace. It is everything that is not Class A, B, C, D or E. It is mostly the low airspace away from airports.

sections.heading: The sport pilot endorsement for controlled airspace (61.325)
points: A sport pilot may not act as pilot in command in Class B, C or D airspace, at an airport in that airspace, or to, from, through or at an airport with an operating control tower, until an authorized instructor has given ground and flight training and a logbook endorsement.

The training covers radios, communications, navigation systems and radar services. It covers operations at a towered airport, including three takeoffs and landings to a full stop, each in the pattern, at an airport with an operating control tower. It also covers the part 91 flight rules for B, C and D airspace and ATC clearances.

The endorsement does not open every airport. A short list of the busiest Class B primary airports (listed in appendix D of part 91) still requires at least a private pilot certificate. Check this before you plan a flight into a large city.
A towered airport can sit in Class E or even Class G airspace. The endorsement is tied to the tower, not only to the airspace letter.

sections.heading: VFR weather minimums (91.155)
points: Class B: 3 statute miles of flight visibility and clear of clouds. Class C and Class D: 3 statute miles, with 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontal clearance from clouds. Class E below 10,000 feet MSL uses the same numbers: 3 miles and 500, 1,000 and 2,000.

Class G at 1,200 feet AGL or less, in the daytime, needs 1 statute mile of visibility and clear of clouds. At night, Class G at that height needs 3 statute miles and the 500, 1,000 and 2,000 foot cloud clearance. Between 1,200 feet AGL and 10,000 feet MSL, Class G follows the day or night rules: 1 mile by day and 3 miles by night, with the 500, 1,000 and 2,000 foot cloud clearance.

In the surface area of Class B, C, D or E airspace, you may not take off, land or enter the traffic pattern unless the ground visibility is at least 3 statute miles. If ground visibility is not reported, flight visibility must be at least 3 statute miles. You also may not operate beneath the ceiling within controlled airspace designated to the surface if the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet.

Your own certificate is stricter than the table. Section 61.315(c)(12) forbids acting as pilot in command when the flight or surface visibility is less than 3 statute miles. So the 1 mile daytime Class G minimum does not help you. Also remember 61.315(c)(13): you must always keep visual reference to the surface.

sections.heading: Altitude and speed limits
points: Your ceiling is 10,000 feet MSL or 2,000 feet AGL, whichever is higher.

Minimum safe altitudes (91.119): always high enough to make an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property if the engine fails. Over a congested area or an open-air gathering, stay 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally. Elsewhere, stay at least 500 feet above the surface. Over open water or sparsely populated areas, stay at least 500 feet away from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure. Powered parachutes and weight-shift-control aircraft may go lower than the 500 foot rule if they do it without hazard to people or property.

Speed limits (91.117): 250 knots indicated airspeed below 10,000 feet MSL. 200 knots at or below 2,500 feet above the surface within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of Class C or D airspace. 200 knots in the airspace under a Class B area or in a VFR corridor through it. These limits rarely stop a sport pilot, but the tests ask for them.

sections.heading: Special use airspace, TFRs and equipment
points: Prohibited areas ban flight. Restricted areas allow flight only with permission from the using or controlling agency, because they hide hazards such as artillery fire or missiles (91.133). Military operations areas, warning areas, alert areas and controlled firing areas are other kinds of special use airspace. They appear on the sectional chart. Learn the symbols and read the legend.
A temporary flight restriction (TFR) closes airspace for events such as wildfires, VIP visits and large sports events. TFRs appear in NOTAMs, so check them in your preflight briefing every time.

Transponder and ADS-B Out are required in Class B and C airspace, inside 30 nautical miles of the busiest airports (the "Mode C veil") from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, and in Class E at or above 10,000 feet MSL excluding the airspace at and below 2,500 feet above the surface. An aircraft that was not originally certificated with an engine-driven electrical system has limited exceptions. Check 91.215 and 91.225 before you fly into these areas.

sections.heading: Right of way and collision avoidance
points: Rule 91.113 starts with see and avoid. When the weather permits, you watch for other aircraft whether you fly under VFR or IFR. If another aircraft has the right-of-way, you give way, and you may not pass over, under or ahead of it unless you are well clear.
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic.

Converging aircraft of the same category: the aircraft on the right has the right-of-way. Head-on or nearly so: both turn right. Overtaking: the aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way, and the overtaking aircraft passes on the right.

Different categories: a balloon has the right-of-way over any other category. A glider has the right-of-way over powered aircraft. An airship has the right-of-way over other powered aircraft, except one towing or refueling. An aircraft towing or refueling another aircraft has the right-of-way over other powered aircraft.

Landing aircraft have the right-of-way over aircraft in flight or on the surface. When two aircraft approach to land, the lower one has the right-of-way, but it may not cut in front of another aircraft on final approach or overtake it.

Class G day, 1,200 AGL or less
numbers.value: 1 SM, clear of clouds (but sport pilots need 3 SM)

numbers.item: Ceiling needed to operate beneath it in a surface area
Speed within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport, at or below 2,500 AGL

numbers.value: 1,000 ft above highest obstacle within 2,000 ft
30 NM around listed airports, surface to 10,000 ft MSL

traps: The 1 mile daytime Class G minimum is not for you. Your sport pilot visibility floor is 3 statute miles.
Class B requires a clearance, not just a radio call. Class C and D require two-way radio contact before you enter. Class E requires neither.
The tower decides the endorsement, not only the airspace letter. A towered airport in Class E still needs 61.325.
The endorsement does not let you land at the listed Class B primary airports. Those need at least a private pilot certificate.
Do not mix up the 3 mile visibility rule at the airport (91.155(d)) with the 1,000 foot ceiling rule (91.155(c)). They are separate rules.
Right-of-way between categories starts with the balloon at the top, not the airplane on the right.

modules.title: Weather: theory, reports, forecasts and the go or no-go decision
modules.summary: How weather forms, which hazards matter to a light aircraft pilot, how to read the reports and forecasts, and how to decide whether to fly.
objectives: Explain pressure, temperature, moisture, stability, fronts and fog in plain terms.
Recognize thunderstorms, wind shear, icing and turbulence and the actions that avoid them.
Read a METAR and find the ceiling, visibility, wind and altimeter setting.
Name the main weather products, including the AIRMET types, and say what each is for.
Make and defend a go or no-go decision, and know what to do after an accidental entry into clouds.

sections.heading: The air around you
points: The standard atmosphere at sea level is 15 degrees C, with a pressure of 29.92 inches of mercury. Temperature falls about 2 degrees C for each 1,000 feet of climb. Pressure falls about 1 inch of mercury for each 1,000 feet. Real air is rarely standard, which is why altimeter settings and density altitude matter.

Sun heats the ground unevenly, and uneven heating moves air. Warm air rises and cooler air flows in. That flow is wind. Wind is also the cause of most surface turbulence, and it shapes your takeoff and landing.

Air holds only so much water vapor. The dew point is the temperature at which the air is full. When the air temperature and the dew point come together, the vapor condenses into cloud or fog. Rising air cools about 5.4 degrees F per 1,000 feet while its dew point falls about 1 degree F, so the two draw together about 4.4 degrees F per 1,000 feet. Divide the temperature and dew point spread in degrees F by 4.4 and multiply by 1,000 to estimate the height of the cloud base above ground level.

Stable air resists vertical motion. It makes layered clouds, steady rain and smooth air, but also poor visibility under a low sky. Unstable air keeps rising once it starts. It makes puffy cumulus clouds, gusty winds, good visibility between clouds, and thunderstorms when the air is moist enough.

sections.heading: Fronts and fog
points: A cold front moves fast. The cooler air shoves under the warmer air and lifts it quickly. Expect a narrow band of heavy weather, gusty winds and sometimes a line of storms, followed by clearing skies and cooler air.
A warm front moves slowly. The warm air slides up over cool air. Expect a wide area of low cloud, steady rain and poor visibility ahead of the front.
A stationary front barely moves, and an occluded front forms when a cold front catches a warm front. Both can bring many hours of poor weather.

Fog forms when the temperature and the dew point come within a few degrees of each other. It is most common on calm, clear nights, over wet ground and in moist air that flows over cooler surfaces. If the spread between temperature and dew point is small and shrinking, expect fog or low cloud. Plan for poor visibility near sunrise.

sections.heading: Hazards you must know
points: Thunderstorms need moist, unstable air and a lifting force. They pass through three stages. A growing cumulus cloud has updrafts. In the mature stage, which begins in about 15 minutes, rain and hail begin to fall, and violent turbulence exists inside and near the cloud. In the dissipating stage, downdrafts spread out. A thunderstorm can bring severe turbulence, hail, lightning, heavy rain, strong wind shear and tornadoes. Light aircraft must stay far away. You cannot see well enough inside a storm to go around it, and you should never plan a path under one.

Wind shear is a sudden, strong change in wind speed or direction over a short distance. Shear near the ground is dangerous because you have little height to recover. A microburst is a small, intense downdraft that spreads out when it hits the ground. An airplane flying through it sees a headwind, then a strong downdraft, then a tailwind. Microbursts are a major hazard near thunderstorms.

Icing builds ice on wings, propeller, windshield and sensors. Light sport aircraft rarely have ice protection. Avoid visible moisture, such as cloud and rain, when the temperature is near or below freezing. Engines can ice up too. Carburetor ice forms when air cools quickly inside the carburetor, so it can occur even when the outside air is above freezing. Use carburetor heat as the manufacturer directs.

Turbulence comes from heat, from wind blowing over hills and buildings, from wind shear and from other aircraft. Strong winds across mountains can create mountain waves and rotors. If you fly in mountains, get training from a mountain-qualified instructor first.
Wake turbulence is air that spins off the wingtips of other aircraft. Cover it in the airport module.

sections.heading: Reading the reports
points: A METAR is an hourly weather report from an airport. It always has the same order: station, day and time in UTC, wind, visibility, weather, sky condition, temperature and dew point, and altimeter setting. Example: KABC 251753Z 24012G20KT 8SM FEW040 BKN070 22/14 A2992. It reads: station KABC, on the 25th day at 1753 UTC, wind from 240 degrees at 12 knots gusting to 20, visibility 8 statute miles, few clouds at 4,000 feet, a broken layer at 7,000 feet, temperature 22 C, dew point 14 C, altimeter 29.92.

The ceiling is the height above ground level of the lowest layer reported as broken or overcast. In the example the ceiling is 7,000 feet. Few and scattered layers are not ceilings. If the sky is totally hidden by ground-based cloud, the vertical visibility is the ceiling.

Weather websites color airports by flight category. Green VFR means a ceiling above 3,000 feet and visibility above 5 statute miles. Blue marginal VFR (MVFR) means a ceiling of 1,000 to 3,000 feet or visibility of 3 to 5 miles. Red IFR means a ceiling of 500 to less than 1,000 feet or visibility of 1 to less than 3 miles. Purple low IFR means a ceiling below 500 feet or visibility below 1 mile. These categories are only a quick look. They are not the legal VFR minimums in 91.155.

A TAF is a forecast for the area within about 5 statute miles of an airport. A PIREP is a pilot report of what other pilots saw in the air. Winds and temperatures aloft forecasts give wind direction (in tens of degrees, true), speed in knots and temperature at set altitudes. Wind speeds in knots convert to miles per hour when you multiply by 1.15.

Advisories warn of hazards. AIRMET Sierra warns of areas of IFR conditions and mountain obscuration. AIRMET Tango warns of moderate turbulence, strong surface winds above 30 knots and low-level wind shear. AIRMET Zulu warns of moderate icing and freezing levels. SIGMETs warn of severe hazards that affect all aircraft, and convective SIGMETs warn of significant thunderstorm activity. Check all of them for your route.

sections.heading: Getting a briefing and deciding
points: Rule 91.103 requires you to become familiar with all available information about your flight. For a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, that includes weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements and alternatives. Get your weather from official sources, such as Flight Service and the Aviation Weather Center. Look at it before you drive to the airport and again before you start the engine.

Make a go or no-go decision on facts. Compare the weather to your own personal minimums, which should be stricter than the legal minimums while you are new. Light aircraft are sensitive to wind. Check the crosswind and gusts against the limit in the flight manual and against your own skill. Do not fly when the forecast gets worse than your training.
Remember that your certificate bars flight without visual reference to the surface and flight with less than 3 miles of visibility. Weather that is legal for another pilot may be illegal for you.

If you lose sight of the natural horizon, treat it as an emergency, even if it happened by accident. The FAA's Airplane Flying Handbook says pilots without current instrument skill often lose control of the airplane in about 10 minutes of flying only by instruments. Do not panic. The first job is to keep the wings level. Trust the instruments instead of your body, trim the airplane for hands-off level flight, and ask ATC for help (121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency). The best answer is never to fly into weather that leads there.

Flight category colors are not the VFR minimums. Use 91.155 for legal minimums, and 61.315 for your own, stricter limits.

Convert knots to miles per hour with 1.15. Do not guess.

Thunderstorms cannot be flown around by eye. Keep far clear.

modules.title: Aerodynamics, stalls, spins and performance
modules.summary: The four forces, angle of attack and stalls, load factor, ground effect, spins, and how density altitude and weight change performance.
objectives: Name the four forces and say how the pilot controls lift.
Explain what a stall is and why it depends on angle of attack, not airspeed.
Use load factor and bank angle to predict stall speed.
Describe spin entry and recovery, and the six steps for a stall recovery.
Explain how density altitude, weight, wind and runway surface change takeoff and landing performance.

sections.heading: Four forces and the controls
points: Four forces act on an aircraft in flight. Lift pulls up, weight pulls down, thrust pushes forward and drag pulls back. In steady, level flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag.

Lift comes from the wing moving through the air. It grows with the square of the airspeed. It also grows with the angle of attack, which is the angle between the wing's chord line and the oncoming air. You control the angle of attack with the elevator or stick.

Drag has two main kinds. Parasite drag rises with speed. Induced drag is a by-product of making lift and is greatest at slow speed and high angle of attack. Together they give a speed with the least total drag, the best glide speed for most aircraft.

The primary controls are the elevator for pitch, the ailerons for roll and the rudder for yaw. Trim takes the pressure off the controls. Flaps raise lift and drag at the same time, so you can fly steeper and slower on approach.

sections.heading: Angle of attack and stalls
points: A wing stalls when the angle of attack goes past a critical value. The smooth airflow over the top of the wing separates, lift drops sharply and the nose usually drops. The wing can stall at any airspeed, in any attitude and with any power setting. The cause is always too much angle of attack.

The first step in every stall recovery is to reduce the angle of attack by pushing forward on the controls. Then level the wings, add power as needed to reach flying speed, and return to the planned flight path. Use the maker's procedure if the flight manual has one. Do not pull up or add power before you lower the angle of attack.

Stalls occur most often in the traffic pattern, where you are low and slow. Typical causes are a steep turn at a low speed, a slip or skid during a turn from base to final, and a pull-up to stretch a glide. Learn to hear and feel the warning signs: a stall warning horn, buffeting, mushy controls and a high nose.

sections.heading: Load factor and stall speed
points: Load factor is the ratio of the lift the wing makes to the weight of the aircraft. It is 1 G in straight and level flight. In a coordinated level turn it goes up with bank. At 60 degrees of bank the load factor is 2 Gs. At 45 degrees it is about 1.4 Gs. At 30 degrees it is about 1.15 Gs.

Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor. At 2 Gs the stall speed is about 41 percent higher. A sport airplane that stalls at 50 knots straight and level stalls at about 71 knots in a level 60 degree banked turn. A 4 G pull makes it stall at 100 knots.

Design maneuvering speed (VA) is the speed below which you can use full deflection of one control, one time, in smooth air, without damaging the airplane. VA is not fixed. It is lower when the airplane is lighter. For many older airplanes it is about 1.7 times the stall speed. Always read it in the flight manual.

sections.heading: Turning tendencies, stability and ground effect
points: A propeller makes four effects that push the nose to one side at high power and low speed: torque reaction, corkscrewing slipstream, gyroscopic action and asymmetric thrust (P-factor). The cure is right rudder when you add power in most single-engine airplanes that spin their propellers clockwise as seen from the cockpit.
Adverse yaw is the tendency of the nose to swing opposite the turn when you roll with the ailerons. The rudder cancels it. Always use coordinated rudder.
A stable airplane tends to return to its trimmed flight condition after a disturbance. Aft loading makes an airplane less stable. Forward loading makes it more stable and a little slower.

Ground effect is a change in airflow when the wing is very close to the ground. Induced drag falls, and the airplane floats. At a height of one wingspan the drop is only about 1 percent. At one-quarter of a wingspan it is about 24 percent, and at one-tenth of a wingspan it is about 48 percent. So the effect is strong only very near the surface. When it ends, as the airplane climbs away, you notice a sink. An airplane can lift off in ground effect at too slow a speed and then settle back. Stay low and accelerate to the climb speed.
Wingtip vortices form behind the wing when it makes lift. They sink and drift with the wind. Heavy, clean, slow airplanes make the strongest vortices. The airport module covers the avoidance rules.

sections.heading: Spins
points: A spin is a stall in which the aircraft also yaws. One wing is deeply stalled and the other is less stalled, so the aircraft rotates as it descends. It follows a stall with an uncoordinated control input, usually too much rudder or too little airspeed in a turn.

The recovery steps vary with the airplane, and the flight manual comes first. If the flight manual has no procedure, the Airplane Flying Handbook gives a six-step template. First reduce power to idle. Second, put the ailerons in neutral. Third, apply and hold full opposite rudder until the rotation stops. Fourth, apply brisk forward elevator to reduce the angle of attack. Fifth, neutralize the rudder after the rotation stops. Sixth, pull back gently to return to level flight, taking care not to stall again or to exceed the G limits.

Rule 61.309(j) lists stall awareness, spin entry, spins and spin recovery techniques among the knowledge areas for sport pilots, "as applicable." Know the entry causes and the recovery steps, even if your training airplane is not approved for spins.

sections.heading: Performance
points: Pressure altitude is the altitude shown when the altimeter is set to 29.92. Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. When density altitude is high, the air is thin. The engine makes less power, the propeller makes less thrust and the wing makes less lift for a given airspeed. Hot, high and humid days are the worst.
Higher density altitude means a longer takeoff roll, a shallower climb and a longer landing roll at a higher ground speed. You can lose a lot of margin on a summer afternoon at a high airport.

More weight does the same. The airplane needs more speed to lift off, makes a longer roll, and climbs more slowly. A headwind shortens the roll, and a tailwind lengthens it. Soft, wet or grassy surfaces, and uphill slopes, lengthen the takeoff roll. Wet runways can cause hydroplaning on landing.

Use the flight manual's performance charts, apply a safety margin, and compare the answer to the runway you will use. Rule 91.103 requires you to know the runway lengths and the takeoff and landing distances for your flight.

Climb speeds: VX gives the greatest height gain per distance and clears obstacles. VY gives the greatest height gain per time. The best-glide speed gives the most distance without power. Learn these speeds for your aircraft and fly them.
