modules.title: Aircraft systems, airworthiness and weight and balance
modules.summary: Engine, fuel, electrical and flight instrument systems, the paperwork and inspections that make an aircraft airworthy, and how to compute weight and balance.
objectives: Describe the engine, ignition, fuel, electrical and propeller systems of a typical sport aircraft.
Explain how the pitot-static system and the gyroscopic instruments work and how they fail.
List the documents and inspections that decide whether an aircraft is airworthy.
Compute weight, moment and center of gravity, and tell if a load is within limits.

sections.heading: Engine, ignition, fuel and propeller
points: Most sport aircraft use a four-stroke piston engine. Each cylinder goes through intake, compression, power and exhaust. Two independent ignition systems (usually magnetos) fire two spark plugs in each cylinder. If one fails, the engine runs on the other, with a small drop in power. You check each system at the engine run-up, and you confirm the drop is within the limits in the flight manual.

A carburetor mixes fuel and air. Fuel injection sprays fuel into the intake directly. A carburetor can ice up because the air cools quickly inside it. This can occur on a day with a warm outside temperature. Carburetor heat melts or prevents the ice. Because heat reduces power, do not leave it on at full power unless the manual says so.

The mixture control sets the fuel and air ratio. A mixture that is too lean at high power can cause detonation. Detonation is an uncontrolled, explosive burn in the cylinder. It overheats the engine and can destroy it. Using a lower fuel grade than the maker requires is another cause. Use the fuel grade the manual specifies. Do not mix grades without authority.

Always check the fuel for water and dirt, with a sampler, from each sump and drain. Check the quantity by eye as well as by gauge. Check oil level before every flight. Avoid fuel exhaustion and fuel starvation, which are two of the most avoidable accident causes. Rule 91.151 requires, for an airplane in VFR, enough fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly 30 minutes by day or 45 minutes at night at normal cruise.

Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide, which is invisible and odorless. A cracked exhaust system can let it into the cabin heater. If you feel a headache, drowsiness or dizziness in flight, turn off the cabin heat, open the vents and land.

Propellers on sport aircraft are fixed pitch, ground adjustable or constant speed. A constant speed propeller is allowed for a sport pilot only after the 61.331 training, unless it is an automated controllable pitch propeller.

sections.heading: Electrical system and avionics
points: A generator or alternator charges the battery and runs the equipment. The battery starts the engine and acts as a backup. A master switch connects the system. If the charging light or ammeter shows a failure, switch off nonessential loads, and plan to land where it is safe. A fuse or circuit breaker protects each circuit.

Some sport aircraft have no engine-driven electrical system at all. Such aircraft enjoy limited exceptions from the transponder and ADS-B rules, but only if they were not originally certificated with such a system.

sections.heading: Flight instruments
points: The pitot-static system feeds three instruments. The airspeed indicator uses pitot (ram) air and static air. The altimeter and the vertical speed indicator use only static air. If the pitot tube blocks and its drain hole stays open, the airspeed reads zero. If the pitot tube and its drain hole both block, the airspeed indicator acts like an altimeter. If the static port blocks, the airspeed reads too low above the blockage altitude and too high below it. The altimeter freezes, and the vertical speed indicator reads zero. Pitot heat and a pitot cover help. Look at the pitot tube and static port on the preflight.

The altimeter shows height from the pressure around it. Set it to the latest altimeter setting. Set it to 29.92 only to find pressure altitude. Altitude errors can come from setting errors and from non-standard temperature.

Gyroscopic instruments include the attitude indicator, the heading indicator and the turn coordinator. A gyro is rigid in space and shows precession. The heading indicator drifts, so compare it to the compass often and reset it. Vacuum or electric power spins the gyros.

The magnetic compass is the simplest instrument and has errors. Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north. Deviation is an error caused by the aircraft's own metal and electrical equipment, noted on a compass card. Turning and acceleration errors add to this. Check the compass against known headings before you rely on it.

Know the airspeed markings. The white arc is the flap operating range, from VS0 (stall speed in the landing configuration) to VFE (maximum flap extended speed). The green arc is the normal range, from VS1 (clean stall speed) to VNO (maximum structural cruising speed). The yellow arc is the caution range. The red line is VNE, the never-exceed speed.

sections.heading: Airworthiness, documents and inspections
points: The pilot in command is responsible for deciding whether an aircraft is in a condition for safe flight (91.7), and for stopping the flight if something goes wrong in the air (91.7(b)). The pilot in command is also the final authority for the flight (91.3).

Rule 91.203 requires an appropriate and current airworthiness certificate and an effective registration, both aboard. The airworthiness certificate must be displayed where passengers and crew can read it. Remember the memory aid AROW: airworthiness certificate, registration, operating limitations (flight manual or placards) and weight and balance data.

Under 91.409(a), no one may operate most aircraft unless it has had an annual inspection within the preceding 12 calendar months. The exceptions in 91.409(c) include aircraft with an experimental airworthiness certificate or a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category. Those aircraft follow their own inspection rules. An aircraft that carries persons for hire, or that an instructor provides for flight instruction for hire, also needs an annual or 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service.
Airworthiness directives are legal orders to fix a known problem. Aircraft must comply with them. A directive can limit a flight.

Required equipment: for an aircraft with a standard airworthiness certificate, rule 91.205(b) lists the equipment needed for daytime VFR. It includes the airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic direction indicator, tachometer, oil pressure and temperature gauges, a fuel gauge, a landing gear position indicator if the gear retracts, safety belts and shoulder harnesses, and an emergency locator transmitter where 91.207 requires one. For other categories, the aircraft's operating limitations and equipment list say what is required.

If something is inoperative, 91.213(d) allows flight in some aircraft only if the item is not required by the type certificate, the equipment list, 91.205 or an airworthiness directive. The item must be removed and placarded or deactivated and placarded, and a pilot or a mechanic must decide it is not a hazard.
At night, 91.209 requires position lights, and requires the anticollision lights to be on if the aircraft has them.

sections.heading: Weight and balance
points: Every aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight and a center of gravity (CG) range in the flight manual. Empty weight is the weight of the aircraft as listed in its weight and balance data. Useful load is the maximum takeoff weight minus empty weight. Fuel, oil, people and baggage all count against the useful load.

Weight times arm equals moment. The arm is the distance from the datum, a reference point set by the maker. The CG is total moment divided by total weight. Aircraft weight and balance computations are also a knowledge area under 61.309(h).
Fuel weighs 6 pounds per gallon for aviation gasoline. 30 gallons weigh 180 pounds, which is more than one passenger.

Worked example. Empty weight 700 pounds at an arm of 30 inches. Two people, 340 pounds, at 36 inches. 20 gallons of fuel, 120 pounds, at 38 inches. Baggage, 20 pounds, at 60 inches. Moments: 21,000 plus 12,240 plus 4,560 plus 1,200 equals 39,000. Total weight is 1,180 pounds. The CG is 39,000 divided by 1,180, which is about 33.05 inches. Compare that to the CG range and the total weight to the limit.

Effects of loading. A CG too far aft makes the aircraft less stable, harder to recover from a stall or spin, and faster. A CG too far forward makes it more stable but slower, and takes more elevator to flare. Overweight loading raises the stall speed and lengthens the takeoff roll.

As you burn fuel, the weight falls and the CG may shift. Check both at the start and the end of the flight. Powered parachutes, weight-shift-control aircraft and balloons hang their load below the lift, so they do not need CG computations. You must still avoid overloading them.

numbers.value: total moment divided by total weight
30 minutes after the first point of landing
within the preceding 100 hours of time in service
white VS0 to VFE; green VS1 to VNO; yellow caution; red line VNE

traps: Weight and balance questions need both numbers: the total weight must be inside the limit, and the CG must be inside the range.
Do not use the weight of fuel in gallons as pounds. Multiply by 6 for aviation gasoline.
A blocked static port changes the airspeed, the altimeter and the vertical speed indicator. A blocked pitot tube changes only the airspeed.
Carburetor ice is possible on a warm day. Do not rule it out because the outside air is above freezing.
The airworthiness certificate does not make the aircraft airworthy forever. The inspections and directives must be current too.
Do not mix up the VS0 and VS1 ends of the arcs. VS0 starts the white arc. VS1 starts the green arc.

read.label: FAA-H-8083-1 Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook

check.q: Which instruments are affected when the static port is blocked?
choices: Airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator
check.why: The airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator all use static pressure. The gyroscopic instruments do not.

check.q: An airplane has an empty weight of 700 pounds at an arm of 30 inches, and carries a 340 pound load at 36 inches, 120 pounds of fuel at 38 inches and 20 pounds of baggage at 60 inches. Where is the CG?
check.why: Total moment is 21,000 + 12,240 + 4,560 + 1,200 = 39,000. Total weight is 1,180 pounds. 39,000 divided by 1,180 is about 33.05 inches.

check.q: How much weight does a pilot remove by burning 10 gallons of aviation gasoline?
check.why: Aviation gasoline weighs 6 pounds per gallon, so 10 gallons weigh 60 pounds.

check.q: A pilot flies at high power with a very lean mixture and notices a rough engine and a high cylinder head temperature. What is a likely cause?
check.why: A very lean mixture at high power, or a lower fuel grade than required, can cause detonation, which overheats the engine.

check.q: What is the fuel reserve rule for an airplane flown VFR at night?
choices: 20 minutes after the first point of landing
30 minutes after the first point of landing
45 minutes after the first point of landing
60 minutes after the first point of landing
check.why: Rule 91.151(a)(2) requires fuel to reach the first point of intended landing and then fly at least 45 minutes at night.

modules.title: Navigation, charts and flight planning
modules.summary: Reading a sectional chart, working out courses and headings, time, speed, distance and fuel, and planning a cross-country flight.
objectives: Read the key features of a VFR sectional chart and know where to find current airport data.
Work out true course, magnetic heading and compass heading from a course, wind and variation.
Solve time, speed, distance and fuel problems, and apply the fuel reserve rule.
Explain pilotage, dead reckoning and the role of GPS and other navigation aids.
Plan a cross-country flight and know what to do if you get lost.

sections.heading: Charts and publications
points: The VFR sectional chart is the chart most sport pilots use. Its scale is 1:500,000, so 1 inch on the chart is about 6.86 nautical miles, or about 8 statute miles. It shows airports, airspace, radio aids, obstacles and terrain. Always check the chart's effective date, and use the legend and the FAA's Aeronautical Chart User's Guide to read the symbols.

Charts show airspace with colored lines. Class B is a solid blue line, Class C a solid magenta line, Class D a dashed blue line and Class E a dashed magenta line where it reaches the surface. A magenta shaded edge marks Class E that begins at 700 feet AGL. A blue shaded edge marks Class E that begins at 1,200 feet AGL. Study the legend on the real chart.
The maximum elevation figure (MEF) printed in each quadrangle gives the height of the highest obstacle or terrain in that area, with a safety margin. Use it for planning a safe altitude.

The Chart Supplement U.S. lists runway lengths, fuel, frequencies, airport hours and remarks. It is published in books by region and revised every 56 days. Check the current edition before you plan a landing at a new airport. Check NOTAMs too, because they list closures and hazards the chart does not.

sections.heading: Position on the Earth
points: Lines of latitude (parallels) run east and west and measure distance north or south of the equator. Lines of longitude (meridians) run north and south and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian. A position is given as latitude and longitude. One minute of latitude equals one nautical mile.

A nautical mile is 6,076 feet. A statute mile is 5,280 feet. A knot is one nautical mile per hour. To change knots into miles per hour, multiply by 1.15. Visibility is in statute miles. Aircraft speed on most airspeed indicators is in knots, and some show miles per hour as well.

sections.heading: Course, heading and variation
points: True course is the direction you want to fly over the ground, measured from true north. Wind pushes you off that line, so you point the nose to one side to cancel the drift. The angle is the wind correction angle (WCA). True heading is true course plus or minus the correction. Add the correction when the wind pushes you left, and subtract it when the wind pushes you right. Think of pointing into the wind.

Magnetic north is not true north. The angle between them is variation, and charts show it on dashed lines called isogonic lines. To change a true heading into a magnetic heading, add west variation and subtract east variation. The memory aid is "east is least, west is best."

The compass has its own errors, called deviation, which come from the metal and electrical equipment on the aircraft. A card near the compass lists corrections. After you correct for deviation you have the compass heading.

The order is: true course, plus or minus WCA, equals true heading. Then plus or minus variation gives magnetic heading. Then plus or minus deviation gives compass heading. Example: true course 090, wind correction 5 degrees to the right, so true heading 095. Variation is 10 degrees east, so magnetic heading is 085.

sections.heading: Time, speed, distance and fuel
points: Distance equals groundspeed multiplied by time. Time equals distance divided by groundspeed. Groundspeed is true airspeed corrected for wind. A headwind lowers it and a tailwind raises it. Example: 60 nautical miles at a groundspeed of 90 knots takes 40 minutes.

Fuel needed equals fuel burn per hour multiplied by time. Include the time for taxi, takeoff and climb as well as cruise. Add the legal reserve and a cushion of your own. Rule 91.151 requires an airplane to carry enough fuel for the first point of intended landing and then 30 minutes by day or 45 minutes at night at normal cruise. For a rotorcraft the reserve is 20 minutes.

Do the calculation twice, once on the ground and again in flight. Compare your actual groundspeed and fuel burn to the plan at each checkpoint. If you are burning more than planned, change your plan before you reach the point of no return.

sections.heading: Pilotage, dead reckoning and electronic aids
points: Pilotage means navigating by looking at landmarks and matching them to the chart. Dead reckoning means navigating by computing from time, airspeed, distance and direction, with the wind included. Most real flights mix the two. Pick checkpoints that are easy to see, such as a lake, a highway intersection or a tower, and space them so you can confirm your position often.

GPS moving maps, tablets and radios make navigation easier, but they can fail. Use them as aids. Keep your chart handy and follow your progress on it. Know where you are, and know what you would do if the screen went blank.

The practical test expects you to be able to plan a cross-country flight, use current charts, pick checkpoints and altitudes, compute headings, time and fuel, and apply information from NOTAMs and the Chart Supplement. You also complete a navigation log and simulate filing a VFR flight plan.

sections.heading: Planning, flight plans and getting lost
points: A VFR flight plan is not normally required within the continental United States, but it is a good safety habit. You open and close it with Flight Service. Control towers do not activate it. If you forget to close it, searchers may be sent for you.

Before you leave, rule 91.103 requires you to review weather, fuel, alternatives, runway lengths and your aircraft's takeoff and landing distances. Plan an alternate in case the weather or fuel changes. Check the weight and balance.

If you become unsure of your position, do not wait. Stay calm and keep flying the aircraft. Climb if it is safe, because height improves your view and your radio range. Use the chart to compare terrain features with where you think you are. Use GPS if you have it. Call ATC or Flight Service, say you are lost and ask for help. Make the call before you are low on fuel, not after.

numbers.value: east is least (subtract), west is best (add)
30 minutes by day, 45 minutes at night
verify position within 3 NM of the planned route; altitude within 200 ft; heading within 15 degrees

traps: East is least, west is best applies when going from true to magnetic. When you go from magnetic to true, you do the opposite.
Use groundspeed, not airspeed, to work out time and fuel.
Do not add the reserve to the trip fuel by guessing. Take the legal minimum and then add your own margin.
A VFR flight plan does not close itself. You must close it with Flight Service.
A nautical mile is longer than a statute mile. Mixing them gives errors of about 15 percent.
Charts show Class E as a magenta or blue shaded edge. Do not confuse these edges with Class D lines.

check.q: The true course is 270 degrees, the wind correction angle is zero and the variation is 12 degrees west. What is the magnetic heading?
check.why: West is best, so you add west variation going from true to magnetic. 270 plus 12 equals 282 degrees.

check.q: A flight of 60 nautical miles is flown at a groundspeed of 90 knots. How long does it take?
check.why: Time equals distance divided by groundspeed. 60 divided by 90 is two thirds of an hour, or 40 minutes.

check.q: How much fuel must an airplane have for a VFR night flight, in terms of reserve?
choices: Enough to reach the first point of intended landing plus 30 minutes
Enough to reach the first point of intended landing plus 45 minutes
Enough for the whole trip plus 1 hour
Enough for the trip with no reserve if there is an alternate
check.why: Rule 91.151(a)(2) requires a 45 minute reserve at night in an airplane.

check.q: Which statement about a VFR flight plan is correct?
choices: The control tower activates it automatically
It is opened and closed with Flight Service
ATC closes it when you land
It is required for every flight in the United States
check.why: The AIM says VFR flight plans are opened and closed with Flight Service, and are not normally required within the continental U.S.

check.q: On a sectional chart, what does the scale 1:500,000 mean in nautical miles for 1 inch?
check.why: On a sectional chart 1 inch equals about 6.86 nautical miles, or about 8 statute miles.

modules.title: Airport operations, radio and wake turbulence
modules.summary: Runway names, markings, signs and lights, the traffic pattern, radio calls at towered and non-towered airports, light gun signals and wake turbulence.
objectives: Read runway numbers, pavement markings, signs and lights.
Fly and describe a standard traffic pattern and the entry to it.
Make radio calls at airports without a tower and at airports with a tower.
Handle a radio failure at a towered airport using light signals.
Avoid wake turbulence and runway incursions.

sections.heading: Runways, markings and signs
points: A runway number is the magnetic direction of the runway centerline, rounded to the nearest 10 degrees, with the last zero dropped. A runway pointing 274 degrees magnetic is runway 27. Its other end is runway 9, because the opposite direction is 94 degrees. Parallel runways add L, R or C for left, right or center.

Runway markings are white. Taxiway markings, and holding position markings, are yellow. A runway holding position marking is four yellow lines, two solid and two dashed, across the taxiway. The solid lines are on the side where you must stop. Never cross them without a clearance from the tower. At an airport with no tower, stop and check for traffic before you enter the runway.

Airport signs help you find your way. A sign with white writing on a red background marks a runway entrance or hold point. Mandatory instruction signs mean stop or hold. A sign with yellow writing on a black background says where you are. A sign with black writing on a yellow background points toward the taxiways or runways you can reach.

A displaced threshold, shown with arrows, is a part of the runway you may use for takeoff, and for landing rollout, but not for touchdown. A wind sock, a wind tee or a tetrahedron shows the wind direction. A segmented circle may show the pattern direction.

sections.heading: Airport lighting
points: The rotating beacon tells you an airport is there at night. A civil land airport shows alternating white and green flashes. A water airport shows white and yellow. Military airports show two quick white flashes between the green flashes. In Class B, C, D or E surface areas, a beacon on in the daytime often means the ground visibility is below 3 miles or the ceiling is below 1,000 feet.

Runway lights and taxiway lights help in the dark. Many small airports have pilot-controlled lighting. You click the microphone on the CTAF frequency a set number of times. The Chart Supplement tells you how.

A PAPI (precision approach path indicator) is a row of two or four lights beside the runway. On the correct glide path you see equal numbers of red and white lights. More red lights mean you are low. More white lights mean you are high. A PAPI gives safe guidance within about 10 degrees of the runway centerline and out to about 3.4 nautical miles from the threshold.

sections.heading: The traffic pattern
points: At an airport without a control tower, powered fixed-wing aircraft turn left in the pattern, unless the airport shows markings or lights that say to turn right (91.126(b)). The legs are upwind, crosswind, downwind, base and final. You depart straight out until you reach the pattern altitude or leave the pattern.

The pattern altitude is usually 1,000 feet above the airport surface for propeller-driven aircraft, unless the Chart Supplement lists something else. Enter at pattern altitude, level, at a 45 degree angle to the downwind leg, abeam the middle of the runway. Avoid straight-in approaches, because they mix with traffic that is already in the pattern.

Fly the same pattern as other traffic, look all around and use the radio. Midair collisions happen most often near airports. Do not descend into the pattern from above. Stay at pattern altitude until you turn base.

Airports in Class D airspace follow the tower's instructions. The tower may ask you to make a right pattern, a short approach or a straight-in approach. If you do not understand, ask. If you cannot do it, say "unable."

sections.heading: Radio at airports without a tower
points: Aircraft at these airports share a common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF). It might be a UNICOM station, a multicom frequency or the tower frequency when the tower is closed. The Chart Supplement lists it. If an airport has no tower and no UNICOM, use 122.9 MULTICOM. Common UNICOM frequencies are 122.7, 122.8, 122.725, 122.975 and 123.0.

The AIM recommends these calls: before you taxi, before you taxi onto the runway, about 10 miles out, when entering downwind, base and final, and when you leave the runway. Radio contact is not a clearance. Look for traffic after each call.

A radio call has four parts. Say who you are calling, who you are, where you are, and what you intend to do. Example: "Greenfield traffic, Sport 123, 10 miles south, descending to 3,000, inbound for landing, Greenfield traffic." Begin with the airport name so listeners know which airport you mean.

sections.heading: Radio at airports with a tower
points: Get the ATIS if there is one. It gives the weather and the active runway. Call ground control before you taxi, and stay on that frequency until the tower tells you to change. Ground frequencies are mostly in the 121.6 to 121.9 MHz range. Tower gives takeoff and landing clearances. Read back all hold-short instructions and runway assignments.

To enter Class D airspace, call before you get there and wait for the controller to answer. Two-way communication exists when the controller replies with your call sign, even if the reply is only "standby." Then you may enter. If the controller answers without using your call sign, such as "aircraft calling Manassas tower, standby," communication is not established and you may not enter. The controller may also tell you to remain outside the airspace.

If the radio fails, you have a plan. Rule 91.129(d)(2) lets a VFR pilot operate in Class D and land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, visual contact with the tower is maintained and a clearance to land is received. Set the transponder to 7600. Watch the tower for light gun signals. Acknowledge them by rocking your wings in the day or by blinking the landing or navigation lights at night.

Light gun signals for an aircraft in flight: steady green means cleared to land. Flashing green means return for landing. Steady red means give way and continue circling. Flashing red means the airport is unsafe, do not land. Alternating red and green means use extreme caution. On the ground: steady green cleared for takeoff, flashing green cleared for taxi, steady red stop, flashing red taxi clear of the runway, flashing white return to starting point.

Emergency transponder codes: 7700 for an emergency, 7600 for radio failure and 7500 for hijacking. Set the code only when it applies, and never pass through these codes by accident while changing the code.

sections.heading: Wake turbulence and runway safety
points: A wing that makes lift makes two spinning tubes of air at its tips. The vortices sink and move with the wind. Large, heavy, slow aircraft make the strongest vortices. They are strongest on a clean wing flying slowly near the ground, so the hazard is highest on takeoff, approach and landing.

Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway: stay at or above its flight path and land beyond its touchdown point. Landing behind a larger aircraft that is departing: land well before its rotation point. Taking off behind a larger aircraft: rotate before its rotation point, and stay above its climb path. After a larger aircraft makes a low approach or touch-and-go, wait at least 2 minutes before you take off or land. A light crosswind can keep the vortices on the runway.

Runway incursions are one of the most serious ground risks. Plan your taxi route before you move. Read the airport diagram. Keep the checklist and the flight bag items stowed during taxi. Never enter an active runway unless you are sure you are cleared and the path is clear. If you are not sure where you are, stop and ask.

numbers.value: 45 degrees to downwind, abeam the midpoint of the runway

numbers.item: Wait after a larger aircraft's low approach or touch-and-go

traps: A radio call is not a clearance at a non-towered airport. Look out the window.
A reply that does not include your call sign does not establish two-way communication. Stay out of Class D (and Class C) until you hear your call sign.
Runway 27 is not 270 degrees true. It is about 270 degrees magnetic.
Beacon colors: white and green means a lighted land airport. White and yellow means a water airport.
A flashing red light gun signal in the air means do not land. A steady red means keep circling.
Wake turbulence plans differ for landing behind and for taking off behind. Do not mix them up.

AIM Chapter 4 Section 1: Navigation aids and traffic advisory practices (CTAF)

check.q: A runway's centerline points 274 degrees magnetic. What is the runway number?
check.why: Round 274 to the nearest 10 (270) and drop the zero. The runway is runway 27.

check.q: You call a Class D tower and the controller answers, "Cessna calling Greenfield tower, standby." Your call sign was not used. May you enter the Class D airspace?
choices: No, two-way communication is not established until the controller uses your call sign
Yes, if you are below 1,000 feet
check.why: Two-way radio communication is established when the controller replies using your aircraft call sign. A reply without it means you may not enter.

check.q: You approach a towered airport and see a steady red light gun signal while you are in flight. What does it mean?
choices: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
check.why: A steady red signal tells an aircraft in flight to give way and continue circling. A flashing red says the airport is unsafe.

check.q: When landing behind a larger aircraft that is landing on the same runway, what should you do?
choices: Stay below its path and land short
Stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point
check.why: Vortices sink behind the larger aircraft. Stay at or above its flight path and land beyond its touchdown point.

check.q: Which direction do you turn in the pattern at an airport with no tower and no special markings?
choices: Right if the wind is from the left
check.why: At airports without an operating control tower, powered fixed-wing aircraft make left turns unless markings or lights show a right pattern.

modules.title: Aeromedical factors, decision making and risk management
modules.summary: How your body reacts to flight, how alcohol and drugs affect you, and the checklists and models pilots use to make safe decisions.
objectives: Explain the causes, symptoms and corrections for hypoxia, hyperventilation, spatial disorientation, motion sickness, ear and sinus problems, carbon monoxide poisoning, fatigue, stress and dehydration.
Describe how alcohol, drugs and medicines affect a pilot.
Use IMSAFE, PAVE, the 3P model and the DECIDE model.
Name the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes.

sections.heading: Oxygen and breathing
points: Hypoxia is a shortage of oxygen reaching the body's tissues. At altitude the air holds the same percentage of oxygen but the pressure is lower, so each breath delivers less. The first effects often include a loss of night vision, even as low as 5,000 feet of cabin pressure altitude. Judgment, memory and coordination are impaired at 12,000 to 15,000 feet. Headache, drowsiness, dizziness and a false sense of well-being are typical. Above 10,000 feet the time of useful consciousness shortens fast. You cannot judge your own condition well, so the sense of feeling fine is a warning sign.

The correction is to descend to a lower altitude, or to use supplemental oxygen. Your sport pilot altitude limits keep you below the altitudes where hypoxia is severe, but some people notice effects early, especially smokers, people with anemia and people who have been drinking or taking certain medicines.

Hyperventilation is breathing faster and deeper than the body needs. It blows off carbon dioxide and causes lightheadedness, tingling in the fingers and toes, and numbness. Stress or fear often triggers it. The symptoms can look like hypoxia. The correction is to slow your breathing on purpose, talk aloud or breathe into a bag. If the symptoms get better, it was hyperventilation. If you have doubt about it, descend.

Carbon monoxide is a gas from engine exhaust that you cannot smell or see. It reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Headache, drowsiness and dizziness in flight, especially with cabin heat on, are warning signs. Shut off the heater, open the vents, use oxygen if you have it, and land. Have the exhaust system checked.

sections.heading: Ears, sinuses, balance and motion sickness
points: As you climb and descend, the pressure in your ears and sinuses must equalize. A cold or sinus infection can block this and cause severe pain. Do not fly with a cold or congestion. If your ears block in a descent, climb a little, clear them and descend more slowly.

Spatial disorientation is the loss of your sense of up. Your inner ear cannot sense small or steady changes in attitude. In cloud or at night without a clear horizon, your senses mislead you. Trust the flight instruments. Avoid flight in conditions without a visible horizon, which is also required by your certificate. Visual illusions at night, such as a sloping runway or a black hole approach, can trick you too.

Motion sickness comes from conflicting signals to your senses. Look outside at the horizon, open the vents, reduce the turbulence by changing altitude and tell your passenger to look out. A passenger who is ill can distract you. Land if needed.

sections.heading: Stress, fatigue, dehydration and night vision
points: Stress adds to the load on your attention. It narrows your focus and makes it hard to see the whole picture. Fatigue slows reactions and decisions and may cause you to skip checklists. Rest before you fly, and do not fly after a sleepless night. Dehydration causes fatigue and headache and can cut your performance. Drink water, especially on hot days.

At night your eyes need time to adapt. Full dark adaptation takes at least 30 minutes in total darkness, though you can reach a moderate level within about 20 minutes under dim red light. Bright lights ruin it. Use dim cockpit lighting, look slightly to one side of a dim object to see it and scan with small eye movements.

Scuba diving adds nitrogen to your blood. The AIM recommends a wait of at least 12 hours before flying to altitudes up to 8,000 feet after diving without decompression stops, and at least 24 hours after diving that needed decompression stops. For flight above 8,000 feet, wait at least 24 hours.

sections.heading: Alcohol, drugs and medicines
points: Alcohol dulls judgment, vision and coordination and makes hypoxia worse. Rule 91.17 sets a minimum of 8 hours after drinking, a limit of 0.04 alcohol concentration, and a ban on flying under the influence. Eight hours is the least. Hangover effects can last longer.

Many prescription and over-the-counter medicines make you drowsy or impair your thinking. This includes antihistamines, cold remedies and pain medicines. Ask your doctor or pharmacist about each new medicine. If you are not sure, do not fly. Rule 91.17(a)(3) bans flying while using a drug that affects your faculties in a way contrary to safety.
The illness or condition that needs the medicine matters as much as the medicine. If you are sick enough to need a drug, think about whether you should be flying at all.

sections.heading: Checklists and models for decisions
points: IMSAFE tests your own fitness before a flight: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion. If any answer worries you, think again about the flight.

PAVE helps you find hazards: the Pilot, the Aircraft, the enVironment and External pressures. The 3P model is Perceive, Process and Perform. First see the hazards. Then judge their effect. Then act to reduce the risk. CARE and TEAM extend the idea. Risk has two parts: how likely it is and how bad it would be.

The DECIDE model is Detect the problem, Estimate the need to react, Choose a course of action, Identify solutions, Do the necessary actions and Evaluate the effects. It is useful when something changes in flight.

Set personal minimums while you are on the ground and calm. Write them down: the lowest ceiling, the lowest visibility, the highest wind and crosswind, the longest flight and the lowest fuel reserve you will accept. Raise them when you are new or tired. Keep to them.

sections.heading: Hazardous attitudes
points: The FAA lists five hazardous attitudes. Anti-authority: "Don't tell me." The antidote is "Follow the rules. They are usually right." Impulsivity: "Do it quickly." The antidote is "Not so fast. Think first." Invulnerability: "It won't happen to me." The antidote is "It could happen to me." Macho: "I can do it." The antidote is "Taking chances is foolish." Resignation: "What's the use?" The antidote is "I'm not helpless. I can make a difference."

Recognize the thought, label it as hazardous and say the antidote to yourself. Pressure from a passenger, a schedule or a wish to look good often hides behind a hazardous attitude. You are the pilot in command, and you can always say no.

at least 30 minutes in total darkness

numbers.value: 12 hours (no decompression stop) or 24 hours (decompression stop)

traps: Hypoxia hides itself. Feeling fine at altitude is not proof you are fine.
Hyperventilation and hypoxia share symptoms. If breathing slowly fixes it, it was hyperventilation. Descend if you doubt it.
Carbon monoxide has no smell. A headache with the heater on is a warning, not a coincidence.
Eight hours after drinking is the legal minimum, not a recommendation to fly at 8 hours.
Over-the-counter medicines can ground you too.
Each hazardous attitude has its own antidote. Match them correctly.

check.q: A pilot feels tingling in the fingers, lightheadedness and a feeling of suffocation during a stressful moment. What is the likely cause, and what is the correction?
choices: Carbon monoxide; turn on the heater
check.why: These are symptoms of hyperventilation. Slowing your breathing helps carbon dioxide return to normal.

check.q: Which hazardous attitude is "It won't happen to me"?
check.why: Invulnerability is the belief that accidents happen to other people. The antidote is "It could happen to me."

check.q: What does the "A" in IMSAFE stand for?
check.why: IMSAFE stands for Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion.

check.q: You feel a headache and drowsiness in flight with the cabin heater on. What should you suspect first?
check.why: Exhaust fumes can leak into the cabin heat. Shut off the heater, open the vents and land.

check.q: A pilot dives with scuba and needs no decompression stop. After how long is it recommended to fly to altitudes up to 8,000 feet?
check.why: The AIM recommends at least 12 hours after dives without decompression stops, and at least 24 hours after dives with decompression stops.

modules.title: Emergencies, pilot authority and accident reporting
modules.summary: How to handle an engine failure, a fire, a radio failure and a forced landing, how to ask for help, and when you must report to the NTSB.
objectives: Describe the actions for an engine failure, including after takeoff.
Describe the first steps for an engine fire, an electrical fire and a cabin fire.
Declare an emergency by radio and by transponder, and know what an ELT does.
Explain a pilot in command's emergency authority under 91.3.
State when the NTSB must be told about an accident or incident.

sections.heading: Fly first, then solve the problem
points: In every emergency the order is: fly the aircraft, then solve the problem, then communicate. Keep the aircraft under control and at a safe speed before you work on the cause.

The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority over, the aircraft (91.3(a)). In an in-flight emergency that needs immediate action, you may deviate from any rule in part 91 as much as the emergency requires. If the FAA asks, you must send a written report of the deviation (91.3(b) and (c)).
Learn your emergency checklists before you need them. Memorize the first few steps. Read the rest from the checklist.

sections.heading: Engine failure
points: If the engine quits in cruise, lower the nose and establish the best glide speed from the flight manual. The practical test expects you to hold that speed within 10 knots. Choose a landing area, preferably into the wind, and plan your approach to it. While you glide, try the checklist items: fuel selector, fuel pump, mixture, carburetor heat, ignition switch and primer. Do not spend all your height on the checklist.

Tell someone. Call on the frequency in use, or on 121.5, say MAYDAY (three times if time permits), your position, your problem and your intentions. Set the transponder to 7700. Tighten your harness and brief your passenger.

If the engine quits soon after takeoff, push the nose down at once to keep flying speed. The safest choice is usually to land straight ahead, or with a gentle turn, on the best surface available. A turn back to the airport is the "impossible turn." It needs enough height, planning and practice, and can end in a stall or a hard landing. Decide on your plan on the ground, before every takeoff.

Plan for the landing. Fly a stabilized approach. Use flaps when you are sure of making the field. When the landing is assured, shut off the fuel and the electrical system as the flight manual directs. Keep the battery master on until you no longer need power for vital systems. Land as slowly as you can, under control.

sections.heading: Fires
points: Engine fire: unless the flight manual says otherwise, shut off the fuel first. Set the mixture to idle cutoff and the fuel selector valve to off. Leave the ignition on so the engine burns off the fuel left in the lines. Do not try to restart the engine if the fire goes out. Land as soon as possible.

Electrical fire: you will usually smell burning insulation. Check circuit breakers, instruments, avionics and lights for the faulty circuit. If you cannot find it, turn off the battery master and alternator or generator switches. Landing as soon as possible is the safest choice.

Cabin fire: it comes from smoking, electrical faults or the heating system. Put out the fire with an extinguisher if you have one, find and shut down the faulty system, then open the vents to clear smoke. If smoke gets worse when the vents open, close them. Descend and land as soon as possible.

sections.heading: Other problems
points: Door opens in flight: most doors do not stay wide open. Concentrate on flying the airplane. Do not release your seat belt to reach the door. Fly a normal pattern and land.

Radio failure: set the transponder to 7600. Near a tower, stay in VFR weather and watch for light gun signals. The airport lesson explains the rule in 91.129(d)(2). Away from a tower, try another radio or frequency, and land at a suitable airport.
Accidental flight into cloud: see the weather lesson. Keep the wings level, trust the instruments and ask for help.
Ballistic parachute: if the aircraft has one, learn the conditions for using it, the arming and disarming steps, and brief any passenger who may need to pull the handle if you cannot.

sections.heading: Asking for help
points: To get help, tell the ATC facility or any station you can reach. Say the nature of the trouble, your intentions and the help you need. A distress call starts with MAYDAY, preferably repeated three times. An urgency call starts with PAN-PAN, used the same way. MAYDAY has absolute priority and tells other stations to keep radio silence on that frequency.
The emergency transponder code is 7700. The radio failure code is 7600. The hijack code is 7500. Radar sites show these codes with an alarm.

An emergency locator transmitter (ELT) sends a signal after a crash. The 406 MHz type is digital and can carry your registration and position. Satellites no longer monitor the older 121.5 and 243.0 MHz types, so those depend on a nearby facility or an aircraft overhead hearing the signal. Test and register your ELT as the maker directs.

sections.heading: Reporting accidents and incidents
points: The operator of an aircraft must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately, by the fastest means available, after an aircraft accident or after certain serious incidents (49 CFR 830.5). The NTSB Response Operations Center numbers are 844-373-9922 and 202-314-6290.

An aircraft accident is an event between the time anyone boards the aircraft with the intention of flight and the time all persons have left it, in which someone suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives substantial damage. A fatal injury is a death within 30 days. A serious injury includes a stay of more than 48 hours in hospital, most broken bones, severe bleeding or tissue damage, damage to an internal organ, and some burns.

Substantial damage is damage that harms the structural strength, performance or flight characteristics of the aircraft and normally needs major repair or replacement of the part. Bent cowling, small dents or holes in skin, and damage limited to landing gear, wheels, tires, flaps or wingtips are not substantial damage.

Serious incidents that need an immediate call include a flight control malfunction or failure, a crewmember unable to do normal duties because of injury or illness, an in-flight fire, a midair collision, damage to property other than the aircraft that is estimated to exceed $25,000, and release of all or part of a propeller blade (not caused by ground contact alone).

After an accident, you also file Board Form 6120 within 10 days. A report on an incident is filed only if the NTSB asks for it. Every crewmember attaches a statement about the facts, conditions and circumstances as soon as physically able.

traps: Engine failure after takeoff: the turn-back is not the default. Straight ahead or a gentle turn is usually the safer choice.
A test answer that says to shut off the ignition first in an engine fire is wrong. Shut off the fuel first, and leave the ignition on to burn off the fuel left in the lines.
You can only break a rule in an emergency to the extent the emergency demands. After that, return to the rules.
NTSB notification is immediate. The written report is due in 10 days. Do not confuse the two.
Substantial damage does not include damage limited to a bent cowling, wingtips, flaps, tires or landing gear.
7600 is radio failure and 7700 is emergency. 7500 is hijack. Do not mix them up.

check.q: An engine fire starts in flight and the flight manual gives no different instruction. What is the first step?
choices: Shut off the fuel by setting the mixture to idle cutoff and the fuel selector to off
Turn off the ignition and the master switch
Dive to blow the fire out
check.why: The Airplane Flying Handbook says to shut off the fuel supply first. The ignition stays on so the engine can use up the fuel left in the lines.

check.q: The engine quits shortly after takeoff. What is generally the safest course?
choices: Turn back to the runway at once
Lower the nose and land straight ahead or with a gentle turn
check.why: Lowering the nose and landing ahead usually gives the lowest risk. The turn back needs enough height and practice.

check.q: Which transponder code means radio failure?
check.why: 7600 means two-way radio failure. 7700 is an emergency and 7500 is a hijack.

check.q: When must the operator of an aircraft first notify the NTSB after an aircraft accident?
choices: Immediately, by the most expeditious means
check.why: Rule 830.5 requires immediate notification of the nearest NTSB office. The Board Form 6120 follows within 10 days.

check.q: A pilot in command may deviate from a part 91 rule in an in-flight emergency. To what extent?
choices: As much as the pilot likes
Only as much as the emergency requires
check.why: Rule 91.3(b) allows a deviation to the extent required to meet the emergency. A written report may be requested.

test_day: Bring a government photo ID with your date of birth, signature and physical address, and your knowledge test report (the AKTR).
Bring your pilot logbook with the instructor's endorsements for the knowledge test and the practical test, and any training records.
Bring proof of medical fitness: a medical certificate or your U.S. driver's license.
Bring your completed application (FAA Form 8710-11 or the IACRA record), your student pilot certificate, and the examiner's fee as agreed ahead of time.
Bring the aircraft's airworthiness certificate, registration, operating limitations or flight manual, weight and balance data and maintenance records. The aircraft must meet 14 CFR 61.316.
Bring current charts, the Chart Supplement, a flight computer or calculator, and a plan for the cross-country flight the examiner assigns.
Sleep well, eat, drink water and arrive early. Follow IMSAFE before you start.
In the oral exam, it is fine to say "I will look that up." Show the examiner how you find the answer in the regulation, the AIM or the flight manual.
after: The examiner issues a temporary certificate. Carry it with your photo ID until your permanent certificate arrives.
Keep your logbook. Your category and class privileges and your endorsements are recorded there.
Plan your flight review within 24 calendar months, and keep three takeoffs and landings in the last 90 days to carry a passenger.
To add night flight, retractable gear, a manual controllable pitch propeller, a VH endorsement or controlled airspace privileges, find an instructor and follow the rules in the aircraft lesson.
To add another category or class, see 14 CFR 61.321.
Next steps: fly with a safety pilot or instructor in new airplanes, set personal minimums, and consider the Recreational or Private Pilot course on this site.
